title: Yeezy
hook: The partner was the product, so when he went, the product went with him.
situation: Adidas and Kanye West, now known as Ye, launched Yeezy in 2015. By 2022 it was one of the most valuable collaborations in sportswear, and the shoes carried his name and design.
exchange: Ye designed the shoes and lent his name. Adidas made, marketed and sold them around the world.
brought: Design teams, factories and global retail.
The designs, the name and a huge following.
turning_point: In October 2022, after a series of antisemitic statements by Ye, Adidas ended the partnership and stopped production. It was left holding a warehouse of shoes with his name on them.
metric_label: Yeezy revenue in 2022, the year Adidas ended the deal
measure: Reported by Adidas. The company sold some of the remaining stock in 2023, which brought in about €750m
evidence: Adidas published the figures in its results. It sold part of the inventory in 2023, gave part of the proceeds to organisations fighting hate, and decided not to write off most of the rest.
lesson: If the product carries a person’s name, plan for the day you have to remove it. Own enough of the design to carry on without them.
take: Adidas did the right thing, and it still cost a fortune. The lesson isn’t to avoid big partners. It’s to know what you own when it ends.

title: Like a Prayer
hook: Pepsi paid for the song, then the music video arrived.
situation: Pepsi had followed Michael Jackson with Madonna. Her new single, ‘Like a Prayer’, would premiere in a Pepsi advert before anyone heard it on the radio.
exchange: Pepsi paid Madonna a reported $5m. Madonna gave Pepsi the first play of her new single, in a gentle advert about childhood memories.
brought: A reported $5m and a global advertising slot.
A new single and the attention of the world.
turning_point: The advert aired in early 1989. The next day Madonna released her own video for the song, with burning crosses and religious imagery. Religious groups threatened a boycott, and Pepsi pulled the advert.
metric_label: Before Pepsi aired the advert again
measure: Pepsi showed an edited version at the 2023 MTV Video Music Awards. A fact, not a result
evidence: The advert, the video and the withdrawal are well documented. No figure shows what the episode cost Pepsi or gained Madonna.
lesson: You can control your advert. You can’t control what your partner makes next. Agree in advance what happens when their work and yours collide.
take: Madonna kept the money and the controversy. Pepsi kept neither, until it decided, decades later, that the story was worth telling.

title: The Superstar in a Rent-a-Car
stage: Ran for two decades and ended
hook: For almost twenty years, a football star ran through airports for Hertz.
situation: Hertz wanted business travellers to see renting a car as fast and easy. O.J. Simpson was one of the most popular athletes in America.
exchange: Hertz paid Simpson to star in its adverts, sprinting through airport terminals to the Hertz counter. Simpson gained fame far beyond football.
turning_point: In June 1994, Simpson was arrested for the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman. Hertz cut its ties with him. He was acquitted in 1995 and later found liable in a civil case.
metric_label: From the first airport advert in 1975 to 1994
measure: The length of the partnership. A fact, not a result
evidence: The campaign and its end are well documented. Hertz never published what the adverts or the end of the partnership did to its business.
lesson: The longer a face represents you, the more completely you are tied to them. Long partnerships need a plan for the worst day.
take: The most successful endorsement of its era became the hardest to watch. Nothing about the adverts changed, only what people knew.

title: The World Cup in Court
hook: After sixteen years, FIFA sold the sponsorship to the rival, and a judge found it had lied.
situation: Mastercard had sponsored the World Cup for sixteen years and believed it had the first right to renew. FIFA was negotiating with Visa at the same time.
exchange: Mastercard paid for its place as the World Cup’s card. FIFA gave it the association with the world’s most watched tournament.
brought: Sponsorship money and sixteen years of loyalty.
turning_point: In 2006 FIFA signed Visa. Mastercard sued in New York, and a judge ruled that FIFA had broken its agreement and misled both companies. In 2007 FIFA settled, Visa kept the rights and Mastercard walked away with a payment.
metric_label: Paid by FIFA to Mastercard to settle
measure: The settlement value reported in 2007. A deal term, not a result
evidence: The court’s findings and the settlement are on the public record, one of the most reliable sources in this edition. What the loss of the World Cup cost Mastercard was never published.
lesson: Loyalty in a contract is only worth what the contract says. Get the right to renew in writing, and check that it binds.
take: Mastercard won in court and lost the World Cup. Sometimes the best outcome of a broken partnership is a cheque and a clean exit.

title: One Photo, Two Sponsors
hook: Kellogg’s dropped the Olympic champion. Subway kept him.
situation: After winning eight gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, Michael Phelps was on cereal boxes across America.
exchange: Kellogg’s paid Phelps to appear on its packs and in its adverts. Phelps gave Kellogg’s the most celebrated athlete of the year.
brought: Money and a place on the breakfast table.
Eight gold medals and a clean, wholesome image.
turning_point: In February 2009 a British newspaper published a photo of Phelps with a bong. Kellogg’s said his behaviour was not consistent with its image and let his contract lapse. The next day Subway said it would keep him.
metric_label: Between Kellogg’s dropping Phelps and Subway keeping him
measure: Two sponsors, one photo and opposite decisions. A fact, not a result
evidence: Both decisions are well reported. Phelps went on to win more medals and more sponsors, and no figure shows what either company gained or lost.
lesson: Decide in advance what your partner could do that you would forgive. The same mistake can be fatal to one partnership and survivable for another.
take: Kellogg’s acted on its image, Subway on its customers. History has been kinder to Subway’s call.

title: The Cost to Shareholders
stage: Dropped by several, kept by one
hook: An economic study put a price on a scandal for the companies that sponsored it.
situation: Tiger Woods was the richest athlete in the world, sponsored by Nike, Gatorade, Accenture, AT&T, Gillette and EA Sports, among others.
exchange: The sponsors paid Woods for his image of discipline and success. Woods gave them the most dominant athlete in sport.
brought: Hundreds of millions in endorsement fees.
Winning, and an image of control.
turning_point: After a car crash outside his home in November 2009, reports of infidelity followed. Accenture, AT&T and Gatorade ended their deals. Nike stayed.
measure: A University of California, Davis study compared sponsors’ share prices with the market and rivals over 13 trading days
evidence: This is the rare failure with a modelled estimate. The economists compared each sponsor with the market and its closest competitor, and warned that the margin of error was large because many sponsors were parts of bigger companies.
lesson: The closer your brand is to the person, the more their scandal costs you. The study found the sports brands lost most.
take: The only modelled effect in this edition measures damage, not gain. That tells you something about what gets studied.
credit: Victor Stango and Christopher Knittel, UC Davis, 2009

title: The Crash
hook: The collaboration was so popular it broke the website.
situation: Target had made cheap designer collaborations its signature. Missoni, the Italian fashion house, was known for colourful zigzag knitwear.
exchange: Missoni designed some 400 products, from clothes to bikes. Target made them affordable and sold them in its stores and online.
brought: Stores across America and low prices.
A famous pattern and Italian fashion credibility.
turning_point: On launch day in September 2011, Target’s website crashed and stayed down for most of the day. Shelves emptied within minutes, and the products appeared on eBay at several times the price.
metric_label: eBay listings by the afternoon of launch day
measure: Listings reported on launch day, many above double the Target price. A sign of demand, not Target’s sales
evidence: The crash and the resale frenzy were widely reported. Target didn’t publish the line’s sales, and the damage was frustrated customers rather than lost money.
lesson: Success can fail too. If a partnership could sell out in minutes, plan for the demand, or the story becomes the people who couldn’t buy it.
take: The only failure here caused by too much love. Customers weren’t angry at Missoni. They were angry they couldn’t get it.

title: The Exodus
hook: The comeback story was the product, and it wasn’t true.
situation: Lance Armstrong had survived cancer and won seven Tours de France. Nike, Trek, Anheuser-Busch and Oakley built campaigns on his story, and Livestrong sold millions of yellow wristbands.
exchange: Sponsors paid Armstrong for his image of courage. Armstrong gave them the most inspiring story in sport.
brought: Seven Tour titles and a survivor’s story.
turning_point: In October 2012 the US Anti-Doping Agency published its evidence of doping. On 17 October Nike ended its contract, saying it had been misled for more than a decade. Trek and Anheuser-Busch followed the same day, and Oakley days later.
metric_label: Yearly income Armstrong could lose, as estimated at the time
measure: A BusinessWeek estimate of what the sponsors leaving could cost Armstrong each year
evidence: The exits are well documented. The figure is an estimate of Armstrong’s loss, not the sponsors’, and no sponsor published what the association had cost it.
lesson: When you buy a story, check it. A partnership built on a person’s character is only as true as their character.
take: Nike said it had been misled. The harder question for every sponsor is how much they wanted to believe.
credit: Nike, Trek, Anheuser-Busch, Oakley and Lance Armstrong

title: Everything Is Not Awesome
hook: A campaign film turned a toy partnership into a question about the Arctic.
situation: LEGO had made Shell-branded sets since 1966, and in the 2010s they were sold at Shell petrol stations in 26 countries. Shell was planning to drill for oil in the Arctic.
exchange: LEGO made Shell-branded toys. Shell sold them at its stations and put LEGO in front of millions of families.
brought: Its bricks and the trust of parents.
Petrol stations and a promotion budget.
turning_point: In July 2014 Greenpeace released a film showing a LEGO Arctic drowning in oil. In October, LEGO said it would not renew the deal, while saying the issue was between Greenpeace and Shell.
metric_label: Views of Greenpeace’s film by October 2014
measure: Views reported at the time. A measure of the campaign against the deal, not of the deal itself
evidence: The film’s reach and LEGO’s decision are documented, and Greenpeace said over a million people emailed LEGO. Neither company published what the partnership earned.
lesson: A partner’s business becomes part of yours. If your customers are children and their parents, you inherit every argument about your partner.
take: LEGO insisted the campaign wasn’t about it. It ended the deal anyway, because a brand built on trust can’t afford the argument.

title: Songs of Innocence
hook: A free album nobody asked for appeared in half a billion libraries.
situation: Ten years after the U2 iPod, Apple was launching the iPhone 6. U2 had a new album and wanted it heard by as many people as possible.
exchange: Apple paid for the album and put it, free, into the iTunes library of every customer. U2 got the widest release in history.
brought: Over 500 million iTunes accounts and a launch event.
turning_point: The album arrived automatically on 9 September 2014. Many customers saw it as an intrusion, and within days Apple released a tool to remove it. Bono later apologised.
metric_label: iTunes accounts the album was added to
measure: Apple’s reach figure. Apple said 33 million people had accessed the album a week later
evidence: The reach is Apple’s own number, and the backlash and removal tool are documented. No figure shows whether either side gained.
lesson: Reach without consent is not reach. A gift people didn’t choose can feel like an intrusion.
take: The same partners as Edition 04, ten years on. In 2004 people chose the U2 iPod. In 2014 the album chose them.
credit: Apple, U2 and Universal Music Group, 2014

title: The Spokesman
hook: For fifteen years, a customer’s story was the brand’s story.
situation: Jared Fogle said he had lost more than half his body weight eating Subway sandwiches. From 2000 Subway built its healthy-eating message around him.
exchange: Subway paid Fogle to be its spokesman. Fogle gave Subway a real customer’s story that made fast food seem healthy.
turning_point: In July 2015 federal agents searched Fogle’s home, and Subway suspended the relationship. In August Subway ended it. Fogle pleaded guilty to child sex abuse and child pornography offences and was sentenced to 15 years and 8 months in prison.
measure: The length of the partnership. A fact, not a result
evidence: The partnership, its end and the conviction are on the public record. Subway didn’t publish what the partnership earned or what its end cost.
lesson: When a person becomes your brand’s story, their private life becomes part of your risk. Check the people you make central to your brand.
take: The hardest case in the archive to write. The partnership worked for years, which is exactly why its end was so damaging.

title: Art Not Oil
hook: Protesters performed in the galleries until the sponsor left.
situation: BP had sponsored Tate since 1990, the longest-running sponsorship of a permanent art collection in Britain. Climate campaigners argued that oil money shouldn’t pay for art.
exchange: BP paid to sponsor Tate’s collection displays. Tate gave BP a place in Britain’s cultural life.
turning_point: Campaign groups such as Liberate Tate staged performances in the galleries for years. In March 2016 BP announced it would end the sponsorship in 2017, citing a challenging business environment rather than the protests.
measure: The length of the partnership. A fact, not a result
evidence: The partnership’s length and end are documented. BP said the protests weren’t the reason, campaigners said they were, and the yearly sums were small compared with Tate’s total income.
lesson: A partnership can lose its licence to operate long before it loses money. Watch what the partner’s audience thinks of you.
take: BP said it was about business. Maybe so. But the reason a sponsor gives for leaving is rarely the whole reason.

title: Mr Big’s Last Ride
hook: A brand agreed to appear in a show, and its bike was part of a character’s death.
situation: HBO’s Sex and the City sequel, And Just Like That, featured a Peloton bike in its first episode. Peloton had agreed to the placement.
exchange: Peloton provided the bike and its instructor. HBO gave Peloton a place in one of the year’s most anticipated shows.
brought: A much-anticipated show and its audience.
turning_point: In the episode, broadcast on 9 December 2021, Mr Big dies of a heart attack after a Peloton class. Peloton’s shares fell. Within days it released its own advert, made with Ryan Reynolds’ agency, showing the character alive, then withdrew it after allegations were made against the actor.
metric_label: Peloton’s share price, overnight after the episode
measure: Reported share price fall. Peloton’s shares were already falling, so the episode was not the only cause
evidence: The share price fall and the quick response are documented. Peloton was already struggling, and its own advert went viral but had little lasting effect on the price.
lesson: A placement in someone else’s story means they decide your role. Ask how your product will be used before you agree.
take: Peloton’s answer was brilliant and fast, and then it had to delete it. It’s a reminder that you never control the people in a partnership, even your own advert.

title: The Arena
hook: A crypto exchange bought trust from sport, and the trust didn’t hold.
situation: FTX wanted ordinary people to trust cryptocurrency. It signed deals with an arena in Miami, Major League Baseball, Formula 1’s Mercedes team and stars such as Tom Brady.
exchange: FTX paid for names on arenas, umpires’ sleeves and adverts with athletes. Sport gave FTX the trust and attention of fans.
brought: Very large sums for naming rights and endorsements.
turning_point: In November 2022 FTX collapsed and filed for bankruptcy. Its founder was later convicted of fraud. A court ended the arena deal, and investors sued many of FTX’s sports partners and celebrity endorsers.
metric_label: How long the 19-year arena deal lasted
measure: From June 2021 to its termination in bankruptcy court in January 2023. A fact, not a result
evidence: The deals, the collapse and the court decisions are on the public record. The lawsuits against partners show the reputational cost, but none has published a loss.
lesson: When a partner pays you to lend them trust, you are part of what they sell. Check where the money comes from.
take: Sport rented its credibility to a company that didn’t deserve it. The money was real, and so was the damage.
credit: FTX, Miami-Dade County and the Miami Heat, 2021 to 2023

title: Yeezy Gap
situation: Gap was searching for relevance. In 2020 it signed a ten-year deal with Kanye West, now known as Ye, who had worked at a Gap store as a teenager.
exchange: Ye designed collections for Gap. Gap manufactured and sold them, and expected the line to earn $1bn within five years.
brought: Stores, manufacturing and a mass audience.
turning_point: In September 2022 Ye’s lawyer told Gap he was ending the deal, saying Gap had broken its promises on stores. Gap said the partners were not aligned. Weeks later Gap pulled the remaining products from stores after Ye’s antisemitic statements.
measure: The time the partnership lasted. A fact, not a result
evidence: The deal, the expected $1bn and the early end are reported. Neither side published the sales the line achieved.
lesson: A long contract doesn’t make a long partnership. Agree how decisions get made before the first collection, not after.
take: Gap wanted culture, Ye wanted control. Neither got what they signed for.
